newsitem.title: USA: Florida whipped by wind gusts of 50 mph.
newsitem.headline: Florida whipped by wind gusts of 50 mph.

text.p: Much of Florida became a virtual wind tunnel Friday with gusts of up to 50 mph burying some coastal roads in sand and briefly knocking out power to more than 6,000 homeowners, but no injuries were reported.

A coastal flood warning was issued for much of the coast from Key West north to Savannah, Ga, nearly 550 miles, because of the powerful surf and 15 foot waves, the National Weather Service said. A portion of state highway A-1A near Fort Lauderdale was closed for several hours after powerful waves dumped piles of sand and debris on the road.
Forecasters said sustained winds were blowing at 35 to 45 mph with gusts at 50 mph. A wind advisory was issued for the entire state but forecasters said winds were blowing hardest in South Florida.

The unusually rough weather was blamed on a combination of an Arctic high pressure system over the Great Lakes and a low pressure system over the Caribbean, National Weather Service forecaster Bob Ebaugh said. Florida lies midway between the two weather fronts.
Florida Power & Light said about 6,000 customers lost power briefly when flying tree limbs and debris snapped electrical wires in some neighborhoods.

National Hurricane Center forecasters were keeping a close eye on the Caribbean front, saying there was a chance it could develop into a late-season tropical depression over the weekend. Most hurricanes typically develop during August but the Atlantic hurricane season officially ends Nov. 30.
Miami Beach's famed strip of Art Deco restaurants were empty as tourists fled the stinging sand and light showers.
The weather kept the U.S. Coast Guard busy with more than a dozen rescue cases, it said.
